periods.activity_title: Which unit fits? Matching lengths to metres and centimetres

tasks_in_class.description: Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for: height of India Gate, handkerchief, well, mobile phone, elephant's trunk, shirt buttons.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure, p.57
tasks_in_class.description: Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari or stole using the double number line.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick class discussion: hold up familiar objects (a ruler, a school bag strap) and ask students to name the unit they would measure each in. Move directly to Let Us Find, p.57 (“Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for: height of India Gate, handkerchief, well....”). Students discuss in pairs, then share answers; the class builds a shared chart of 'small things — cm / big things — m'.

Introduce the double number line drawn on the board (cm on one rail, m on the other). Work through Different Units but Same Measure, p.57 (“Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari or stole....”). Students point to matching pairs and articulate why 300 cm and 3 m name the same length, surfacing the ×100 relationship.

Consolidation: pose two fresh matching problems aloud — ‘Is 500 cm the same as 5 m?’ and ‘Would you measure a bus in cm or m?’ — and ask students to write their reasoning in one sentence. Close by having two students read their sentences aloud; the class thumbs-up or corrects.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is choosing cm for large objects simply because centimetres feel more familiar — watch for students who write ‘cm’ for India Gate or a well. Use the double number line as a visual anchor: point out that moving one step right on the metre rail equals one hundred steps on the cm rail. This multiplicative relationship, established here, underpins every conversion in the chapter.
materials: Blackboard or chart paper for double number line
Small classroom objects (pencil, book, bag strap)

periods.activity_title: Stepping into kilometres — playground measure and table

tasks_in_class.description: Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground with long tape; walk lines and count steps; use step-distance relationship to find distances of at least 3 locations; identify nearest and farthest from home; write distances in increasing order; name a location ≥1,000 m away.
Complete the table: for each rope length (100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m), find how many ropes are needed to make 1 km.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the kilometre with a brief discussion: ‘We measured handkerchiefs in cm and doorways in m — what unit would we use for the distance from school to the railway station?’ Establish that 1,000 m = 1 km. Mention the long tape, rodometer, and laser distance meter as professional tools.

Take the class to the playground. Use the long tape to mark a 100 m line and a 200 m line. Students walk each line counting their steps; each records their personal step count. Back in class, students use their step-distance relationship to estimate distances to at least three locations (Let Us Do, p.59 — “Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground; use step-distance to find distances....”). They write locations in increasing order and name one that is at least 1,000 m away.

Work through Let Us Explore, p.59 (“Complete the table: for each rope length, find how many ropes make 1 km.”). Students complete individually, then compare with a partner. Draw out the pattern: 1,000 ÷ rope length = number of ropes, reinforcing the km definition multiplicatively.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the km definition — they may write 100 m = 1 km rather than 1,000 m = 1 km. During the rope table, prompt: ‘How many 100 m ropes fit in 1,000 m?’ to let them discover the answer by counting rather than guessing. The step-counting activity grounds the abstraction of a kilometre in a physical, personal reference that students can recall when solving problems.
materials: Chalk or flags to mark the playground

section_titles: Kilometre race — applying km in context
periods.activity_title: Planning a 3-km race — stations, marshals, and flags

tasks_in_class.description: Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race — how many stations? At what positions from the start?
Children at 300 m intervals to direct runners in 3-km race — how many children needed? At what positions from the start?
Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m in a 3-km race — how many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?

time_bands.activity: Draw a horizontal number line on the board labelled 0 to 3,000 m. Ask: ‘If we convert 3 km entirely to metres, how many metres is that?’ Establish 3 km = 3,000 m as the working length for all three tasks, and invite students to suggest what 500 m looks like on the line.

Students solve Let Us Do Q1, p.60 (“Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race....”) and Q2, p.60 (“Children at 300 m intervals to direct runners....”) in their notebooks. For each, they list the positions from the start and count placements. Pairs check each other's position lists before sharing with the class.

Tackle Let Us Do Q3, p.60 (“Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m in a 3-km race....”). Students first find the total number of flag positions (3,000 ÷ 50 = 60 gaps, so 60 placements after start), then decide the alternating colour pattern. Discuss: does the colour at the finish line matter? Confirm answers as a class and note the total red and blue flag counts.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is counting intervals rather than positions — students who find 6 intervals for Q1 may write 6 stations rather than counting the actual placements. Encourage drawing the number line with positions marked; this makes the interval-vs-position distinction visible. In Q3, students may wonder whether the start counts as a flag placement — let them argue both interpretations, then follow the book's answer key.

section_titles: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
periods.activity_title: Vivek Express — reading a distance table and computing

tasks_in_class.description: Find the total length of the route from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari.
Find the distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road.
Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?
Find the distance between Guwahati and Coimbatore JN.

homework.description: Find the distance between Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to open their books to the Vivek Express distance table on p.61. Spend time reading the table together: which column gives cumulative distance from Dibrugarh? How do we find the distance between two intermediate stations? Establish the subtraction method: distance between two stops = larger cumulative distance minus smaller.

Students solve Longest Train Journey Q1, p.61 (“Find the total length of the route....”) and Q2, p.61 (“Find the distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road.”) independently, showing working in column form. Volunteers share and the class checks the subtraction.

Work through Q4, p.61 (“Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?”) as a class reasoning task: students compute both distances, compare, and write a sentence explaining their answer. Close with Q5, p.61 (“Find the distance between Guwahati and Coimbatore JN.”) completed individually. Q3 is noted as a take-home practice item.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently try to read a single-column distance as a between-station gap rather than a cumulative figure — clarify that each number shows distance from Dibrugarh, so between-station distance always requires subtraction. Q4 is a comparison task that requires two subtractions and a final comparison; encourage students to write both results before deciding. Additional practice: Longest Train Journey Q3, p.61.
materials: Textbook open to p.61 (Vivek Express distance table)

section_titles: The world of small things — millimetre
periods.activity_title: Zooming in — discovering the millimetre on a ruler

tasks_in_class.description: Examine the scale markings between 1 cm and 2 cm; count mm marks; discover 1 cm = 10 mm.
Measure the lines in the geometric design and write their measurements in cm and mm.

homework.description: Soak moong/chana seeds; over 4 days take one seed each day and measure sprout length in mm; record in table.

time_bands.activity: Give every student a ruler. Ask: ‘Between the 1 cm mark and the 2 cm mark, how many small lines do you see?’ Students count and record; the class converges on 10 small divisions. Work through Let Us Explore, p.61 (“Examine the scale markings between 1 cm and 2 cm; count mm marks; discover 1 cm = 10 mm.”). Students write the discovery sentence in their own words.

Students complete Let Us Measure, p.61 (“Measure the lines in the geometric design and write their measurements in cm and mm.”). They place the ruler carefully, read the whole-cm mark, then count residual mm marks, and record in the format ‘_ cm _ mm’. Pairs compare readings; disagreements are resolved by re-measuring together.

Consolidation: ask two or three students to report one line's measurement and explain how they read the ruler — whole cm first, then leftover mm marks. Briefly introduce the seed-sprouting task (Let Us Do, p.62) as an extended observation to begin at home: soak seeds tonight and measure the sprout daily for four days, recording in mm. Students note this in their homework diary.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error is counting the cm marks rather than the small divisions between them — a student who counts 9 dividing lines rather than 10 spaces will conclude 1 cm = 9 mm. Demonstrate by pointing to the space between two adjacent small marks and calling it ‘one millimetre’. The seed-sprouting task is set as an extended home observation; students should bring their recorded tables when the relationships section is taken up.
materials: Small seeds (moong or chana) and a cup of water for the home task introduction

periods.activity_title: The full metric ladder — drawing, scaling, and converting

tasks_in_class.description: Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm in notebook using a scale.
Fill in the blanks in the cm↔mm double number line (1 cm/10 mm to 50 cm/__ mm).

Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm; 514 mm to cm mm; 6 m 34 cm to cm; 20 m 12 cm to cm; 397 m to cm; 5,792 cm to m cm; 9,108 cm to m cm; 34 km to m; 6,870 m to km m; 10,552 m to km m; 29 km 30 m to m; 32 km 359 m to m.

homework.description: Fill in the blanks in the m↔cm double number line (1 m/__ cm to 21 m/__ cm).
Fill in the blanks in the km↔m double number line (1 km/1,000 m to 82 km/__ m).

time_bands.activity: Display the relationship box on the board: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1,000 m = 1 km. Students copy it. Then tackle Let Us Draw, p.62 (“Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm....”) — each student places the ruler and draws the line, converting compound lengths to mm as needed before marking.

Complete Let Us Do Q1(a), p.63 (“Fill in the blanks in the cm↔mm double number line....”) as a class: fill the first two entries together, then students complete the rest independently. The ×10 pattern should emerge; ask: ‘What do you multiply cm by to get mm?’

Students work through Let Us Do Q2, p.63–64 (“Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm....”) in their notebooks. Work the first two conversions on the board as models (one direction each), then students continue independently. Monitor for systematic multiply/divide errors. The double-number-line tasks for m↔cm and km↔m (Q1(b) and Q1(c)) are assigned as reinforcement to complete at home.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent error is multiplying when dividing is needed — for example, converting 89 mm to cm by multiplying by 10 to get 890 rather than dividing to get 8 cm 9 mm. Anchor the direction: ‘going to a bigger unit means fewer of them, so divide’. The full conversion drill in Q2 covers all four units and both directions; additional double-number-line practice from Q1(b) and Q1(c) is provided as home reinforcement.

periods.activity_title: Adding and subtracting compound lengths — two strategies

tasks_in_class.description: Rani has ribbon rolls of 3 m 75 cm and 2 m 25 cm. How much ribbon in total?
Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?
Gulmarg Gondola section 1 is 2 km 300 m and section 2 is 2 km 650 m. Find total distance covered.
Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs: 11 mm vs 1 cm; 26 mm vs 2 cm; 20 cm vs 201 mm; 1,020 mm vs 1 m; 2 m vs 245 cm; 5,678 m vs 6 km; 6 km 1,480 m vs 7 km 479 m.

time_bands.activity: Model two strategies on the board using a simple example (2 m 40 cm + 1 m 80 cm): Strategy 1 — add like units separately and regroup (240 cm + 180 cm = 420 cm = 4 m 20 cm done in column with m and cm columns); Strategy 2 — convert both to cm first, add, then convert back. Show both layouts side by side. Ask students which strategy they prefer and why.

Students solve Let Us Do Q1, p.66 (“Rani has ribbon rolls of 3 m 75 cm and 2 m 25 cm....”), Q2, p.66 (“Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal....”), and Q3, p.66 (“Gulmarg Gondola section 1 is 2 km 300 m and section 2 is 2 km 650 m....”) independently, choosing their preferred strategy. Volunteers write their working on the board.

Work through Let Us Do Q4, p.66 (“Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs: 11 mm vs 1 cm; 26 mm vs 2 cm....”). Students must first convert both lengths to the same unit to compare, then subtract. Do the first pair as a class; students complete the remaining six independently.

periods.teacher_notes: Regrouping errors are common in subtraction — when the smaller unit of the minuend is less than the subtrahend's smaller unit, students must borrow (e.g. 48 km 700 m − 17 km 900 m requires borrowing 1 km = 1,000 m). Pause on Q2 and ask: ‘Is 700 m enough to subtract 900 m from? What do we do?’ Q4 tests comparison before subtraction; students who skip conversion will circle the wrong length.

periods.activity_title: Scaling lengths — cloth, road, and thread problems

tasks_in_class.description: Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m. Use the double number line to find cost or length for various quantities up to ₹2,000.
Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border. How much thread for 5 m sari? Thread costs ₹50 per metre — how much money needed?
Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days. How much road is laid each day?

time_bands.activity: Model the multiplication strategy for compound lengths on the board: 1 m 80 cm × 3 = (1 m × 3) + (80 cm × 3) = 3 m + 240 cm = 3 m + 2 m 40 cm = 5 m 40 cm. Similarly show division: 4 m 80 cm ÷ 4 = (4 m ÷ 4) + (80 cm ÷ 4) = 1 m 20 cm. Ask students to identify which operation matches each word problem context.

Students complete Let Us Do Q2, p.67 (“Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m. Use the double number line to find cost or length....”). Draw the double number line (metres on one rail, rupees on the other) on the board; students fill in entries by scaling the given rate. Pairs compare and justify each entry.

Students solve Q3, p.67 (“Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border. How much thread for 5 m sari?....”) — a two-step problem requiring unit conversion and then cost calculation — and Q4, p.67 (“Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days....”). For Q4, encourage the strategy of dividing km and m separately before recombining. Volunteers share working.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q3, students often miss that a 5 m sari border is equivalent to two 50 cm lengths per metre — encourage them to draw a line diagram marking 50 cm intervals. In Q4, the division of 12 km 600 m by 6 works cleanly (2 km 100 m), but students who convert entirely to metres risk arithmetic errors; both strategies are valid and the board model should show each. The proportional reasoning in Q2 prepares students for ratio work in later chapters.

periods.activity_title: Feet, inches, and estimation — measuring ourselves and our world

tasks_in_class.description: Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch; note 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, 1 foot = 12 inches or 30 cm.
Stand against wall, mark your height; measure distance floor-to-mark in feet and inches; find tallest student in class and their height in feet and inches.
Estimate the height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood; height of the tallest tree; depth of a well or swimming pool — share reasoning and reference used.

time_bands.activity: Students take out their rulers. Ask: ‘Does your ruler show any markings other than centimetres?’ Explore Let Us Explore, p.68 (“Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch....”). Students count the cm marks that fit in one inch space and record: 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm; 1 foot = 12 inches = 30 cm.

Carry out Try This, p.69 (“Stand against wall, mark your height; measure floor-to-mark in feet and inches....”). In groups of three, one student stands against the wall, a second marks the height, and the third measures with a ruler or tape. Each student records their own height in feet and inches; groups identify their tallest member.

Students work through Let Us Estimate Q1–Q3, p.68 (“Estimate the height of the tallest building; height of the tallest tree; depth of a well....”). For each, they identify a reference (a storey is about 3 m; an electric pole is about 8 m) and use it to reason to an estimate, writing both the reference and the estimate. Two or three students share their reasoning; the class discusses whether the reference choices are sensible.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often round 1 inch to exactly 2 cm, losing the 5 mm; stress that the measurement is 2 cm 5 mm and that this precision matters when measuring height in feet and inches. For the estimation tasks, the key teaching move is insisting on a named reference — ‘I estimated using a single-storey house (about 3 m)’ — rather than an unanchored guess. Sharing different references for the same object shows that estimation is a reasoned strategy, not a random number.

periods.activity_title: Operation-sign puzzle — reasoning with all four operations

tasks_in_class.description: Put appropriate operation signs (+, –, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid such that each row, column, and 4×4 box does not repeat any sign.

time_bands.activity: Warm up with a brief oral review: ask students to convert two quantities aloud — ‘3 km 200 m to metres’ and ‘6 m 45 cm to cm’ — as a mental exercise to activate the conversion relationships. Take answers and correct quickly.

Introduce Try This (puzzle), p.69 (“Put appropriate operation signs (+, −, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid such that each row, column, and 4×4 box does not repeat any sign.”). Students attempt the puzzle individually; then form groups of three to compare partial solutions and reason together about which sign must go where. Groups share their logic, not just their final grid.

Whole-class share: one group explains a row or column they are confident about and why each sign belongs there. The class verifies the completed grid together. Close by asking: ‘Which constraint — row, column, or box — was hardest to satisfy?’ — inviting students to articulate their reasoning strategy.

periods.teacher_notes: The puzzle is a constraint-satisfaction problem; students who try to fill in random signs quickly find contradictions — encourage them to see this as useful information (elimination). If the class reaches a consensus solution quickly, extend by asking: ‘Is there more than one valid arrangement?’ The oral conversion warm-up at the start of this unit draws on the cm↔m and km↔m equivalences established earlier in the chapter, tying the procedural and reasoning strands together as a natural close.
materials: Textbook open to p.69 (Try This puzzle)
Student notebooks or worksheets with blank 4×4 grids

items.prompt: Riya walked along the school boundary and counted 1,200 steps. Earlier, she found that 100 steps cover 80 m. How far did Riya walk? Write your answer in metres and also in kilometres and metres.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1,200 steps × 80 m per 100 steps = 960 m, which is 0 km 960 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the personal step-distance relationship to convert step count to metres, then express in km and m.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students may draw a number line marking each 100-step group; those who finish can find how many more steps Riya would need to reach exactly 1 km.

exercise.description: Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground with long tape; walk lines and count steps; use step-distance relationship to find distances of at least 3 locations; identify nearest and farthest from home; write distances in increasing order; name a location ≥1,000 m away.

items.section_title: The world of small things — millimetre
items.prompt: Look at the ruler markings below. Between the 3 cm mark and the 4 cm mark there are 10 small divisions. Sana measures a leaf and finds it reaches the 6th small mark after 4 cm. Write the leaf's length in cm and mm, and also in mm only.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The leaf ends at 4 cm and 6 mm, so its length is 4 cm 6 mm, which is 46 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the whole centimetre, count the leftover millimetre marks, then convert: cm × 10 + mm = total mm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Let struggling students physically count tick marks on a real ruler; confident students can measure a second object in the classroom and record both forms.

exercise.description: Measure the lines in the geometric design and write their measurements in cm and mm.

items.section_title: The world of small things — millimetre
items.prompt: A student counts 10 small divisions between the 2 cm mark and the 3 cm mark on a ruler. What does each small division represent?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1 mm, because 10 equal divisions span 1 cm and 1 cm = 10 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 1 cm equally by the number of divisions: 1 cm ÷ 10 = 1 mm per division.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses the small division with the centimetre unit itself, not recognising the finer scale.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplies rather than divides, reversing the direction of the relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student halves 1 cm instead of dividing by 10, perhaps thinking of 2 mm per division.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Let struggling students count divisions on a real ruler between two cm marks; stretch: ask what 3 small divisions equal in mm and in cm mm.

exercise.description: Examine the scale markings between 1 cm and 2 cm; count mm marks; discover 1 cm = 10 mm.

items.prompt: A student finds that 1 inch on a ruler equals 2 cm 5 mm. How many millimetres is 1 inch?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 25 mm, because 2 cm = 20 mm and 5 mm more gives 25 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert the cm part to mm (2 × 10 = 20), then add the mm part (20 + 5 = 25).

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student writes 2 cm 5 mm as 205 by placing digits side by side without converting cm to mm.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student converts 2 cm to 20 mm but ignores the 5 mm, losing the compound part.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplies 2 cm 5 mm by 10 as a whole (treating the compound as 25 cm rather than 2 cm 5 mm).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use a ruler to count mm marks in one inch space; stretch: convert 6 inches to cm and mm.

exercise.description: Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch; note 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, 1 foot = 12 inches or 30 cm.

items.prompt: Ravi stands against the wall and his height is marked. He then measures from the floor to the mark and finds it is 4 feet 3 inches. Given that 1 foot = 30 cm and 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, write Ravi's height in centimetres.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 feet = 4 × 30 cm = 120 cm; 3 inches = 3 × 2 cm 5 mm = 6 cm 15 mm = 7 cm 5 mm; total = 120 cm + 7 cm 5 mm = 127 cm 5 mm, which may be written as 127.5 cm or 127 cm 5 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert feet to cm (multiply by 30) and inches to cm and mm (multiply by 2 cm 5 mm), then add the results.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can first convert just the feet part and write that answer, then add the inches part separately; stretch: express the same height in mm only.

exercise.description: Stand against wall, mark your height; measure distance floor-to-mark in feet and inches; find tallest student in class and their height in feet and inches.

items.prompt: Which unit is most appropriate to measure the length of a swimming pool?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Metres, because a swimming pool is a large object measured conveniently in metres — a standard pool is about 25 m or 50 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Match the size of the object to the unit: large objects use metres; very large distances use kilometres; small objects use centimetres or millimetres.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student defaults to centimetres for any physical object, not distinguishing between small and large scales.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student chooses the smallest unit, perhaps confusing precision with appropriateness.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student overestimates the pool's length, applying km which is used for distances between places.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can be given a list of reference sizes (a fingernail, a door, a field, a city) and asked to match each to a unit first; stretch: name two objects at school best measured in each of the four units.

exercise.description: Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for: height of India Gate, handkerchief, well, mobile phone, elephant's trunk, shirt buttons.

items.prompt: A stole is 250 cm long. Which of the following shows the same length in metres?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 m 50 cm, because 200 cm = 2 m and 50 cm remain, giving 2 m 50 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide total cm by 100 to find whole metres; the remainder is the leftover centimetres.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student divides by 10 instead of 100, confusing the cm-to-m factor with the mm-to-cm factor.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student divides by 1,000 (the km factor) instead of 100.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplies by 10 instead of dividing, moving in the wrong direction.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use the double number line (cm on one rail, m on the other) to locate 250 cm; stretch: convert 375 cm to metres and centimetres.

exercise.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure, p.57
exercise.description: Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari or stole using the double number line.

items.prompt: A rope is 200 m long. How many such ropes placed end to end are needed to make exactly 1 km? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 ropes, because 1 km = 1,000 m and 1,000 ÷ 200 = 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total metres in 1 km (1,000) by the rope length to find the count.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can draw 5 boxes of 200 m each and count to 1,000; stretch: find how many ropes of 150 m are needed for 1 km and whether they fit exactly.

exercise.description: Complete the table: for each rope length (100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m), find how many ropes are needed to make 1 km.

items.section_title: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
items.prompt: On a train route, the distance from the starting station to Station P is 430 km, and to Station Q is 680 km. The distance from the starting station to Station R is 510 km, and to Station S is 820 km. Which pair of stations is farther apart — P and Q, or R and S? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: P to Q: 680 − 430 = 250 km. R to S: 820 − 510 = 310 km. R and S are farther apart.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the smaller cumulative distance from the larger for each pair, then compare the two differences.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can mark P, Q, R, S on a number line and count the gap; stretch: find how much farther apart R and S are compared to P and Q.

exercise.description: Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?

items.prompt: Which is the greater length — 3 m or 280 cm?

options.label: A
options.text: 280 cm, because 280 is a larger number than 3

options.label: B
options.text: 280 cm, because centimetres are smaller units so more of them means a bigger length

options.label: C
options.text: 3 m, because 3 m = 300 cm which is greater than 280 cm

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 m is greater, because converting to the same unit gives 3 m = 300 cm, and 300 cm > 280 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert both lengths to the same unit (cm), then compare the numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student compares the face values of the numbers (280 vs 3) without converting to a common unit.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may have mistakenly converted 3 m as 280 cm or simply guessed equality.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student reasons correctly that cm are smaller units but draws the wrong conclusion — more cm does mean a longer length, so the logic has a partial truth that leads to an error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can convert 3 m to cm on the double number line before comparing; stretch: find the difference between the two lengths in cm.

exercise.description: Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs: 11 mm vs 1 cm; 26 mm vs 2 cm; 20 cm vs 201 mm; 1,020 mm vs 1 m; 2 m vs 245 cm; 5,678 m vs 6 km; 6 km 1,480 m vs 7 km 479 m.

items.prompt: A shop sells ribbon at ₹80 for every 4 m. Complete the table to find the cost for 8 m, 12 m, and 20 m of ribbon.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the unit rate (₹80 ÷ 4 = ₹20 per m), then multiply by each length.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can add ₹80 repeatedly (4 m at a time) using the double number line; stretch: find how many metres of ribbon can be bought for ₹500.

exercise.description: Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m. Use the double number line to find cost or length for various quantities up to ₹2,000.

items.prompt: A single storey of a building is about 3 m tall. A building has 4 storeys. Estimate its height in metres. Is the building likely to be taller or shorter than a 15 m electric pole? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Estimated height: 4 × 3 m = 12 m. 12 m is shorter than 15 m, so the building is likely shorter than the electric pole.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of storeys by the reference height per storey, then compare with the known height.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can draw 4 stacked blocks each labelled 3 m; stretch: estimate how many storeys a 24 m building would have.

exercise.description: Estimate the height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood; height of the tallest tree; depth of a well or swimming pool — share reasoning and reference used.

items.prompt: A 4×4 grid must have exactly the four operation signs +, −, ×, ÷ with no sign repeated in any row or column. One row already shows: + | ÷ | ? | −. Which sign must go in the blank? Explain how you decided.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: × must go in the blank, because + , ÷, and − are already in that row and × is the only remaining sign.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List the four signs, cross out the three already placed in the row, and the remaining one is the answer.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can write all four signs and cross out those already present; stretch: use the same elimination method on a column that has only two signs placed.

exercise.description: Put appropriate operation signs (+, –, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid such that each row, column, and 4×4 box does not repeat any sign.

items.prompt: What is 7 cm 4 mm expressed in millimetres?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 74 mm, because 7 cm = 70 mm and 70 + 4 = 74 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the cm part by 10 to convert to mm, then add the remaining mm.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student multiplies the entire compound number (74) by 10, treating 7 cm 4 mm as 74 cm.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student drops the mm part and only records the cm digit, losing the conversion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student writes 7 in the hundreds place and 4 in the units place, confusing the place-value structure with unit conversion.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use the double number line (cm↔mm) from the textbook to look up 7 cm; stretch: convert 74 mm back to cm and mm as a check.

exercise.description: Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm in notebook using a scale.

items.prompt: Convert 4,500 m to km and m.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 km 500 m, because 4,500 ÷ 1,000 = 4 remainder 500.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the total metres by 1,000; the quotient is km and the remainder is m.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student divides by 100 instead of 1,000, confusing the km factor with the m-to-cm factor.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student divides 4,500 by 1,000 correctly for the km part but then uses 5 instead of 500 for the remainder, dropping two zeros.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student separates the digits 4 and 500 without performing division, misreading place value.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can use the km↔m double number line to find 4,000 m = 4 km then add the remainder; stretch: convert 4 km 500 m back to m as a verification step.

exercise.description: Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm; 514 mm to cm mm; 6 m 34 cm to cm; 20 m 12 cm to cm; 397 m to cm; 5,792 cm to m cm; 9,108 cm to m cm; 34 km to m; 6,870 m to km m; 10,552 m to km m; 29 km 30 m to m; 32 km 359 m to m.

items.section_title: Kilometre race — applying km in context
items.prompt: In a 2 km race, water stations are placed every 400 m, starting 400 m from the start and including the finish line. How many water stations are there in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 water stations, at 400 m, 800 m, 1,200 m, 1,600 m, and 2,000 m (finish).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 2 km to 2,000 m, then divide by the interval (2,000 ÷ 400 = 5) to find the number of stations.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can draw a number line from 0 to 2,000 and mark every 400 m; stretch: find the positions if stations are placed every 250 m in the same 2 km race.

exercise.description: Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race — how many stations? At what positions from the start?

items.section_title: Kilometre race — applying km in context
items.prompt: In a 2 km race, red and blue flags are placed alternately every 100 m, with a red flag at the 100 m mark. How many blue flags are there up to and including the finish line at 2,000 m?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: There are 20 flag positions (100 m, 200 m, …, 2,000 m). Red flags are at odd positions (1st, 3rd, …, 19th) — 10 red flags. Blue flags are at even positions (2nd, 4th, …, 20th) — 10 blue flags.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find total positions (2,000 ÷ 100 = 20), then split equally between red (odd positions) and blue (even positions).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can list flag positions and colour them alternately R, B, R, B; stretch: find the colour of the flag at the 1,500 m mark.

exercise.description: Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m in a 3-km race — how many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?

items.section_title: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
items.prompt: A train travels from City A to City D. The distances from City A are: City B — 320 km, City C — 750 km, City D — 1,100 km. What is the total distance from City A to City D?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1,100 km. The distance from A to D is read directly as the cumulative distance given for City D.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The cumulative distance from the starting city to City D gives the total route length directly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can mark A, B, C, D on a number line using the given values; stretch: find the distance between City B and City C.

exercise.description: Find the total length of the route from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari.

items.section_title: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
items.prompt: Using the same table: City A to City B is 320 km, and City A to City C is 750 km. What is the distance between City B and City C?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the cumulative distance of the nearer city from that of the farther city.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can place B and C on a number line and count the gap; stretch: find the distance from City B to City D.

exercise.description: Find the distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road.

items.prompt: Meena has two pieces of wire. The first is 2 m 65 cm long and the second is 1 m 55 cm long. What is the total length of both pieces of wire together?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 m 20 cm. Adding like units: 65 cm + 55 cm = 120 cm = 1 m 20 cm; 2 m + 1 m + 1 m (carried) = 4 m; total = 4 m 20 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add cm parts first and regroup into metres, then add all metre parts.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can convert both lengths to cm (265 + 155 = 420 cm) then convert back; stretch: if Meena cuts 75 cm from the total, how much wire remains?

exercise.description: Rani has ribbon rolls of 3 m 75 cm and 2 m 25 cm. How much ribbon in total?

items.prompt: Town X to Town Y is 35 km 300 m. A milestone is 14 km 800 m from Town X. How far is the milestone from Town Y?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 35 km 300 m − 14 km 800 m. Since 300 m < 800 m, borrow 1 km: 1,300 m − 800 m = 500 m; 34 km − 14 km = 20 km; answer = 20 km 500 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract like units, borrowing 1 km (= 1,000 m) when the m part of the minuend is smaller than the subtrahend's m part.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can convert both distances to m first (35,300 − 14,800 = 20,500 m = 20 km 500 m); stretch: verify by adding the answer back to the milestone distance to check it equals the total route.

exercise.description: Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?

items.prompt: Priya needs 2 m of thread for every 1 m of embroidery border. The border is 3 m 50 cm long. Thread costs ₹40 per metre. How much will Priya spend on thread?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Thread needed = 2 × 3 m 50 cm = 7 m 00 cm = 7 m. Cost = 7 × ₹40 = ₹280.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the border length by the thread ratio to find total thread, then multiply by the cost per metre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can break the multiplication into 2 × 3 m and 2 × 50 cm separately; stretch: find how much thread Priya would need if the border were 4 m 75 cm long.

exercise.description: Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border. How much thread for 5 m sari? Thread costs ₹50 per metre — how much money needed?

items.prompt: A road 9 km 600 m long is to be built in 8 equal daily sections. How long is each daily section?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 9 km 600 m ÷ 8: 9 km ÷ 8 = 1 km remainder 1 km = 1,000 m; 1,000 m + 600 m = 1,600 m; 1,600 m ÷ 8 = 200 m. Each section = 1 km 200 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the km part, convert any remainder to m and add the remaining m, then divide the combined m part.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling students can convert 9 km 600 m to 9,600 m and divide; stretch: check by multiplying 1 km 200 m × 8 to verify the total.

exercise.description: Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days. How much road is laid each day?
